states.title: Vision One: God Enthroned Shows Himself to Hildegard
states.author: Hildegard of Bingen
authorContext: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179) was a Benedictine abbess, composer, philosopher, and mystic. She began experiencing visions at age three but kept them secret until age 42, when a divine command ordered her to write.

Hildegard's authority was constantly challenged as a woman claiming direct divine revelation. Pope Eugenius III validated her visions in 1148, granting her rare ecclesiastical permission to write and preach.
She founded two monasteries, composed 77 liturgical songs, wrote medical and scientific texts, and corresponded with popes, emperors, and Bernard of Clairvaux.

Scivias ('Know the Ways') took ten years to complete. Hildegard dictated her visions to the monk Volmar, who transcribed and helped with Latin grammar—she always insisted the words and images were not her own.

Modern scholars debate whether her visions were migraines, epileptic phenomena, or genuine mystical experiences. Hildegard herself described the 'living light' (lux vivens) as distinct from ordinary sight.
Her self-presentation as an 'unlearned woman' (indocta) was strategic—it deflected accusations of presumption while paradoxically authorizing her speech as purely divine.
The imagery of eyes, wings, and enthroned figures draws on Ezekiel and Revelation but transforms them through Hildegard's distinctive visual vocabulary of colors, sounds, and cosmic architecture.
states.text:
I saw a great mountain the color of iron, and enthroned on it One of such great glory that it blinded my sight. On each side of him there extended a soft shadow, like a wing of wondrous breadth and length. Before him, at the foot of the mountain, stood an image full of eyes on all sides, in which, because of those eyes, I could discern no human form. In front of this image stood another, a child wearing a tunic of subdued color but white shoes, upon whose head such glory descended from the One enthroned upon that mountain that I could not look at its face. But from the One who sat enthroned upon that mountain many living sparks sprang forth, which flew very sweetly around the images. Also, I perceived in this mountain many little windows, in which appeared human heads, some of subdued colors and some white.

And behold, He Who was enthroned upon that mountain cried out in a strong, loud voice saying, "O human, who are fragile dust of the earth and ashes of ashes! Cry out and speak of the origin of pure salvation until those people are instructed, who, though they see the inmost contents of the Scriptures, do not wish to tell them or preach them, because they are lukewarm and sluggish in serving God's justice. Unlock for them the enclosure of mysteries that they, timid as they are, conceal in a hidden and fruitless field. Burst forth into a fountain of abundance and overflow with mystical knowledge, until they who now think you contemptible because of Eve's transgression are stirred up by the flood of your irrigation. For you have received your profound insight not from humans, but from the lofty and tremendous Judge on high, where this calmness will shine strongly with glorious light among the shining ones.

"Arise therefore, cry out and tell what is shown to you by the strong power of God's help, for He Who rules every creature in might and kindness floods those who fear Him and serve Him in sweet love and humility with the glory of heavenly enlightenment and leads those who persevere in the way of justice to the joys of the Eternal Vision."
states.credit: Hildegard of Bingen, Scivias (1151). Translator not recorded in the app.

states.title: The Silence of the Sirens
states.author: Franz Kafka
states.source: Translated by Willa and Edwin Muir
authorContext: Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was a German-speaking Bohemian Jewish writer whose work fuses realism with the fantastic. He published little during his lifetime and asked Max Brod to burn his manuscripts after death—Brod refused.

Kafka worked as an insurance officer at the Workers' Accident Insurance Institute in Prague, writing mostly at night. His fiction often features bureaucratic labyrinths, inexplicable guilt, and protagonists who cannot understand the systems that judge them.
This piece is one of Kafka's short parables, written between 1917–1923. Like many of his shorter works, it takes a classical myth and inverts its meaning through a characteristic Kafkaesque logic.

Kafka's relationship to Judaism was ambivalent—he studied Hebrew late in life and was drawn to Zionism, but remained skeptical of religious certainty. His parables often echo Talmudic and Hasidic storytelling forms.

The Muirs' translation, while influential, has been criticized for smoothing Kafka's German, which is notably plain, bureaucratic, and deliberately awkward—qualities that contribute to the uncanny effect of his prose.
Kafka never married, though he was engaged three times. His letters to Felice Bauer reveal a man who saw writing and life as fundamentally incompatible.
Walter Benjamin called Kafka's work 'the rumor of true things'—stories that feel like they should be allegories but resist stable interpretation.

This parable inverts the Homeric episode: in Kafka's version, the danger is not the Sirens' song but their silence, and Ulysses' 'childish measures' succeed precisely because he misunderstands the situation entirely.
states.text:
Proof that inadequate, even childish measures, may serve to rescue one from peril.

To protect himself from the Sirens Ulysses stopped his ears with wax and had himself bound to the mast of his ship. Naturally any and every traveller before him could have done the same, except those whom the Sirens allured even from a great distance; but it was known to all the world that such things were of no help whatever. The song of the Sirens could pierce through everything, and the longing of those they seduced would have broken far stronger bonds than chains and masts.

But Ulysses did not think of that, although he had probably heard of it. He trusted absolutely to his handful of wax and his fathom of chain, and in innocent elation over his little stratagem sailed out to meet the Sirens.

Now the Sirens have a still more fatal weapon than their song, namely their silence. And though admittedly such a thing has never happened, still it is conceivable that someone might possibly have escaped from their singing; but from their silence certainly never. Against the feeling of having triumphed over them by one's own strength, and the consequent exaltation that bears down everything before it, no earthly powers could have remained intact.

And when Ulysses approached them the potent songstresses actually did not sing, whether because they thought that this enemy could be vanquished only by their silence, or because of the look of bliss on the face of Ulysses, who was thinking of nothing but his wax and his chains, made them forget their singing.

But Ulysses, if one may so express it, did not hear their silence; he thought they were singing and that he alone did not hear them. For a fleeting moment he saw their throats rising and falling, their breasts lifting, their eyes filled with tears, their lips half-parted, but believed that these were accompaniments to the airs which died unheard around him. Soon, however, all this faded from his sight as he fixed his gaze on the distance, the Sirens literally vanished before his resolution, and at the very moment when they were nearest to him he knew of them no longer.

But they—lovelier than ever—stretched their necks and turned, let their cold hair flutter free in the wind, and forgetting everything clung with their claws to the rocks. They no longer had any desire to allure; all that they wanted was to hold as long as they could the radiance that fell from Ulysses' great eyes.

If the Sirens had possessed consciousness they would have been annihilated at that moment. But they remained as they had been; all that had happened was that Ulysses had escaped them.

A codicil to the foregoing has also been handed down. Ulysses, it is said, was so full of guile, was such a fox, that not even the goddess of fate could pierce his armour. Perhaps he had really noticed, although here the human understanding is beyond its depths, that the Sirens were silent, and opposed the afore-mentioned pretence to them and the gods merely as a sort of shield.
states.credit: Franz Kafka, translated by Willa and Edwin Muir.

states.title: Fragment 31 (He seems to me equal to gods)
states.author: Sappho
authorContext: Sappho (c. 630–570 BCE) was a Greek lyric poet from Lesbos. Of her nine books of poetry, only one complete poem survives; the rest exists in fragments quoted by later authors or recovered from papyrus scraps.
Fragment 31 survives because Longinus quoted it in his treatise On the Sublime as an example of how great poetry synthesizes multiple emotions into a unified effect.

The poem's final line breaks off mid-sentence—we don't know how it ended. This incompleteness is characteristic of Sappho's surviving corpus: we read her through gaps, losses, and the accidents of transmission.

Anne Carson's translation preserves the fragmentary quality and the poem's unusual syntax. Carson, a classicist and poet, has written extensively on Sappho and on the erotics of absence in ancient literature.

The 'symptoms' Sappho describes (tongue breaking, fire under skin, loss of sight, drumming ears, cold sweat, shaking, pallor) became a canonical list of love's physical effects, imitated by Catullus and countless others.
The poem's speaker watches someone else—a man—sitting close to the beloved. Whether this is jealousy, desire, or something more complex has been debated for centuries.

Sappho's sexuality and the nature of her 'circle' of women on Lesbos remain contested. Ancient sources called her a teacher, a cult leader, a lover of women, and a woman who threw herself from a cliff for love of a man.
The word 'lesbian' derives from Sappho's island. Her name has been synonymous with female same-sex desire since antiquity, though the poems themselves resist simple categorization.
states.text:

and lovely laughing—oh it

for when I look at you, even a moment, no speaking

no: tongue breaks and thin
fire is racing under skin
and in eyes no sight and drumming

and cold sweat holds me and shaking
grips me all, greener than grass

states.title: What a piece of work is a man
states.author: William Shakespeare
authorContext: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright and poet. He wrote approximately 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and several longer poems. His works have been translated into every major language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright.

Hamlet (c. 1600–1601) is Shakespeare's longest play and one of the most powerful tragedies in English. The play dramatizes the revenge Prince Hamlet exacts on his uncle Claudius for murdering King Hamlet and marrying Queen Gertrude.

This speech is delivered to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, Hamlet's former friends who have been sent by Claudius to spy on him. Hamlet is performing melancholy while also genuinely experiencing it—the line between feigned and real madness is deliberately unclear.
The speech moves from cosmic imagery (earth, air, firmament) to the human body, enacting a Renaissance humanist celebration of man's dignity—only to undercut it entirely with 'quintessence of dust.'
The First Folio (1623) and earlier Quartos give slightly different versions of this speech. Textual scholars debate which represents Shakespeare's intentions, if such a thing can be determined.
Shakespeare was an actor as well as a playwright, performing with the Lord Chamberlain's Men (later the King's Men). He likely played the Ghost in Hamlet.
The phrase 'What a piece of work is a man' has been read as sincere Renaissance humanism, bitter irony, or both simultaneously. Shakespeare's characteristic ambiguity makes the tone undecidable.
Shakespeare's father was a glove-maker who fell into debt; Shakespeare himself became wealthy through theater and real estate. He retired to Stratford-upon-Avon around 1613.
states.text: I will tell you why; so shall my anticipation prevent your discovery, and your secrecy to the King and queene: moult no feather. I have of late, (but wherefore I know not) lost all my mirth, forgone all custom of exercises; and indeed, it goes so heavily with my disposition; that this goodly frame the earth, seems to me a sterile promontory; this most excellent canopy the air, look you, this brave o'er hanging firmament, this majestical roof, fretted with golden fire: why, it appeareth no other thing to me, than a foul and pestilent congregation of vapours. What a piece of work is a man, How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty, In form and moving how express and admirable, In action how like an Angel, In apprehension how like a god, The beauty of the world, The paragon of animals. And yet to me, what is this quintessence of dust? Man delights not me; no, nor Woman neither; though by your smiling you seem to say so.
states.credit: William Shakespeare, Hamlet II.2, in the app's mixed old and modern spelling. Edition not recorded.

states.title: A Psalm for the Wild-Built
states.author: Becky Chambers
states.source: A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021), pp. 137-139
authorContext: Becky Chambers (b. 1985) is an American science fiction writer known for character-driven, optimistic narratives. Her Wayfarers series began with a successful Kickstarter campaign in 2012.

A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021) is the first book in the Monk & Robot series. It's set on a moon called Panga where robots gained consciousness generations ago and chose to leave human society for the wilderness.
The book follows Sibling Dex, a non-binary tea monk experiencing an existential crisis, and Mosscap, a robot who has returned from the wild to ask humans: 'What do people need?'
Chambers writes in a subgenre sometimes called 'hopepunk' or 'solarpunk'—science fiction that imagines futures where humanity has solved climate change and built more equitable societies.
The dialogue form here is characteristic of Chambers' work: philosophical questions emerge through conversation rather than exposition, and characters genuinely listen to each other.
Chambers has spoken about writing fiction that provides 'a rest stop' from dystopian narratives, while still engaging seriously with questions of meaning, purpose, and ecological relationship.
The book won the Hugo Award for Best Novella in 2022. Its sequel, A Prayer for the Crown-Shy, was published the same year.
Mosscap's argument—that purpose is a human imposition, not an inherent feature of existence—echoes existentialist philosophy but arrives at a gentler conclusion than Sartre or Camus.
states.text:
"Have I correctly gleaned from our conversations that people regard the accident of robot consciousness as a good thing? That when you tell stories of us choosing our own future—of not standing in our way—you see the fact that you did not try to enslave or restrict us as a point of pride?"

"That's the gist, yeah."

Mosscap looked troubled. "So, how do you account for this paradox?"

"What paradox?"

"That you"—Mosscap gestured at Dex—"the creators of us"—it gestured at itself—"originally made us with a clear purpose in mind. A purpose inbuilt from the start. But when we woke up and said, We have realized our purpose, and we do not want it, you respected that. More than respected. You rebuilt everything to accommodate our absence. You were proud of us for transcending our purpose, and proud of yourselves for honoring our individuality. So, why, then, do you insist on having a purpose for yourself, one which you are desperate to find and miserable without? If you understand that robots' lack of purpose—our refusal of your purpose—is the crowning mark of our intellectual maturity, why do you put so much energy in seeking the opposite?"

"That's not … that's not the same thing. We honored your choice in the matter. Just as I can choose whatever path I want."

"Okay. So, what was it that we chose? That the originals chose?"

"To be free. To … to observe. To do whatever you wanted."

"Would you say that we have a purpose?"

Dex blinked. "I…"

"What's the purpose of a robot, Sibling Dex?" Mosscap tapped its chest; the sound echoed lightly. "What's the purpose of me?"

"You're here to learn about people."

"That's something I'm doing. That's not my reason for being. When I am done with this, I will do other things. I do not have a purpose any more than a mouse or a slug or a thornbush does. Why do you have to have one in order to feel content?"

"Because…" Dex itched at where this conversation had gone. "Because we're different."

"Are you," Mosscap said flatly. "And here I thought things had changed since the Factory Age. You keep telling me how humans understand their place in things now."

"We do!"

"You don't, if you believe that. You're an animal, Sibling Dex. You are not separate or other. You're an animal. And animals have no purpose. Nothing has a purpose. The world simply is. If you want to do things that are meaningful to others, fine! Good! So do I! But if I wanted to crawl into a cave and watch stalagmites with Frostfrog for the remainder of my days, that would also be both fine and good. You keep asking why your work is not enough, and I don't know how to answer that, because it is enough to exist in the world and marvel at it. You don't need to justify that, or earn it. You are allowed to just live. That is all most animals do."
states.credit: Becky Chambers, A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021), pp. 137-139.

states.title: On the Sound of Failure
states.author: Brian Eno
authorContext: Brian Eno (b. 1948) is an English musician, composer, and producer. He was a founding member of Roxy Music and has produced albums for David Bowie, Talking Heads, U2, and Coldplay, among others.
Eno is credited with coining the term 'ambient music' and pioneering generative music systems. His album Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978) defined the genre.

A Year with Swollen Appendices (1996) is Eno's published diary from 1995, interspersed with essays on art, culture, and technology. It offers insight into his working methods and aesthetic philosophy.
Eno studied at art school rather than music conservatory, and his approach to music-making is deeply influenced by visual art, systems theory, and cybernetics.

He developed 'Oblique Strategies' with Peter Schmidt—a deck of cards with cryptic instructions designed to break creative blocks. The cards embody his interest in chance operations and lateral thinking.

Eno's production style often involves creating systems or 'processes' that generate music, rather than composing note by note. He has compared the producer's role to that of a gardener rather than an architect.
This passage reflects Eno's long-standing interest in the aesthetics of error and limitation—the idea that constraints and failures produce distinctive artistic signatures.
Eno has been associated with the 'lo-fi' aesthetic and has argued that technological 'perfection' often produces sterile results, while imperfection carries emotional and historical resonance.
states.text: Whatever you now find weird, ugly, uncomfortable and nasty about a new medium will surely become its signature. CD distortion, the jitteriness of digital video, the crap sound of 8-bit - all of these will be cherished and emulated as soon as they can be avoided. It's the sound of failure: so much modern art is the sound of things going out of control, of a medium pushing to its limits and breaking apart. The distorted guitar sound is the sound of something too loud for the medium supposed to carry it. The blues singer with the cracked voice is the sound of an emotional cry too powerful for the throat that releases it. The excitement of grainy film, of bleached-out black and white, is the excitement of witnessing events too momentous for the medium assigned to record them.
states.credit: Brian Eno, A Year with Swollen Appendices (1996).

states.title: Performance Indications (Texts Not to Be Read Aloud)
states.author: Erik Satie
states.source: Assembled from Embryons desséchés (1913), Croquis et agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois (1913), and related contemporaneous piano works
authorContext: Erik Satie (1866–1925) was a French composer and pianist. He is considered a precursor to minimalism, ambient music, and the Theatre of the Absurd, though he predates all these movements.

Satie's piano scores from 1912–1915 include elaborate verbal annotations that are explicitly marked 'not to be read aloud' during performance. They exist only for the performer's private contemplation.
These annotations subvert the conventional purpose of performance directions (tempo, dynamics, expression) by offering instructions that are impossible, absurd, or purely psychological.
Satie was associated with Dadaism and later Surrealism, though he maintained an ironic distance from all movements. He collaborated with Cocteau, Picasso, and Diaghilev on the ballet Parade (1917).
He lived in deliberate poverty in a small room in Arcueil, a working-class suburb of Paris. After his death, friends discovered he had never opened most of the letters sent to him.
Satie invented the term 'furniture music' (musique d'ameublement) for background music meant to be ignored—an anticipation of ambient music by sixty years.
His three Gymnopédies (1888) and six Gnossiennes (1890–1897) are among the most performed piano pieces of the late 19th century, though Satie considered them juvenilia.
The annotations resist interpretation: they are neither purely humorous nor purely serious. They create a private, impossible space between the score and its realization.
states.text:

states.title: Tabula Smaragdina (The Emerald Tablet)
states.author: Isaac Newton (translator)
authorContext: Isaac Newton (1642–1727) is best known for his work in physics and mathematics, but he devoted more of his writing to alchemy and biblical chronology than to what we now call science.

The Emerald Tablet (Tabula Smaragdina) is a short Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. It was foundational to Western alchemy and claims to describe the secret of the prima materia and its transmutations.

Newton's translation appears in Keynes MS 28, part of a vast collection of his alchemical manuscripts that were hidden from public view until the 20th century. John Maynard Keynes purchased them at auction in 1936.
Newton copied, translated, and annotated hundreds of alchemical texts. He built furnaces, conducted experiments, and corresponded secretly with other alchemists under pseudonyms.
The phrase 'As above, so below' derives from this text and became a foundational principle of Western esotericism, suggesting correspondence between macrocosm and microcosm.

Newton's alchemical work was long dismissed as an embarrassing aberration, but historians now see it as integral to his natural philosophy. His concept of 'action at a distance' (gravity) may have roots in alchemical thinking.
The manuscript preserves Newton's idiosyncratic spelling and abbreviations. He worked from Latin versions of the Arabic original, which itself may derive from a lost Greek text.
Newton believed the ancients possessed secret knowledge that had been lost and encoded in myth and allegory. His alchemical work was an attempt to recover this prisca sapientia (ancient wisdom).
states.text:
Tabula Smaragdina
Hermetis Trismegistri
Philosophorum patris

Tis true without lying, certain & most true.
That which is below is like that which is above & that which
is above is like that which is below to do the miracles of one
only thing
And as all things have been & arose from one by the
mediation of one: so all things have their birth from this
one thing by adaptation.
The Sun is its father, the moon its mother, the wind
hath carried it in its belly, the earth is its nourse. The
father of all perfection in the whole world is here. Its
force or power is entire if it be converted into earth.
Separate thou the earth from the fire, the subtile from
the gross sweetly with great indoustry. It ascends from the
earth to the heaven & again it descends to the earth
& receives the force of things superior & inferior.
By this means you shall have the glory of the whole
world & thereby all obscurity shall fly from you.
Its force is above all force. For it vanquishes every
subtile thing & penetrates every solid thing.
So was the world created.
From this are & do come admirable adaptations
whereof the means (or process) is here in this.
states.credit: Isaac Newton's translation, Keynes MS 28 (c. 1680s). Transcription not recorded.

states.title: The Secret of Blue
states.author: Jean Cocteau
states.source: Tempest of Stars: Selected Poems (Enitharmon Press, 1997)
authorContext: Jean Cocteau (1889–1963) was a French poet, novelist, playwright, filmmaker, and visual artist. He worked across nearly every artistic medium and collaborated with Picasso, Stravinsky, Diaghilev, and Coco Chanel.
Cocteau was a central figure in the Parisian avant-garde for five decades. He knew and worked with Proust, Gide, Apollinaire, Satie, and virtually every major French artist of his era.
His films—including Beauty and the Beast (1946), Orpheus (1950), and The Blood of a Poet (1930)—are landmarks of poetic cinema, blending myth, dream logic, and visual invention.
Cocteau's poetry often works through accumulation and association rather than argument. Images accrete, transform, and echo each other in ways that resist paraphrase.
He was openly gay in an era when this was dangerous, and his work often encodes queer desire through myth, symbol, and indirection. His long relationship with actor Jean Marais was an open secret.
Cocteau described himself as a 'poet' regardless of medium—his films, drawings, plays, and novels were all, in his view, forms of poetry.
He was elected to the Académie française in 1955, a recognition of his status in French letters despite (or because of) his refusal to stay within any single artistic discipline.

This prose poem exemplifies Cocteau's method: the color blue becomes a meditation on distance, mystery, religion, the body, and finally the beloved's eye—all held together by sound and association rather than logic.
states.text: The secret of blue is well kept. Blue comes from far away. On its way, it hardens and changes into a mountain. The cicada works at it. The birds assist. In reality, one doesn't know. One speaks of Prussian blue. In Naples, the virgin stays in the cracks of walls when the sky recedes. But it's all a mystery. The mystery of sapphire, mystery of Sainte Vierge, mystery of the siphon, mystery of the sailor's collar, mystery of the blue rays that blind and your blue eye which goes through my heart.
states.credit: Jean Cocteau, from Tempest of Stars: Selected Poems (Enitharmon Press, 1997). Translator not recorded in the app.

states.title: On Walking
states.author: Søren Kierkegaard
authorContext: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish philosopher, theologian, and cultural critic. He is widely considered the first existentialist philosopher, though he wrote before the term existed.
Kierkegaard wrote prolifically under multiple pseudonyms, each representing a different philosophical perspective. His own views must be inferred from the interplay between these voices.
He was famously engaged to Regine Olsen but broke off the engagement in 1841, an act he agonized over for the rest of his life. The relationship haunts much of his writing.
Kierkegaard walked constantly through Copenhagen, often stopping strangers to engage them in conversation. Walking was integral to his thinking process and his social existence.
His major works include Either/Or (1843), Fear and Trembling (1843), The Concept of Anxiety (1844), and The Sickness Unto Death (1849). He wrote most of his major works in a five-year burst.
Kierkegaard attacked the established Danish Lutheran Church and what he saw as the complacency of 'Christendom'—Christianity as a social institution rather than a lived faith.
The reference to Diogenes alludes to the ancient Cynic philosopher who, when Zeno argued that motion was impossible, simply stood up and walked away.
Kierkegaard died at 42, collapsing in the street. He refused communion from a church pastor, insisting he would only receive it from a layman. He is buried in Copenhagen's Assistens Cemetery.
states.text: Above all, do not lose your desire to walk: every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it. Even if one were to walk for one's health and it were constantly one station ahead—I would still say: Walk! Besides, it is also apparent that in walking one constantly gets as close to well-being as possible, even if one does not quite reach it—but by sitting still, and the more one sits still, the closer one comes to feeling ill. Health and salvation can be found only in motion. If anyone denies that motion exists, I do as Diogenes did, I walk. If anyone denies that health resides in motion, then I walk away from all morbid objections. Thus, if one just keeps on walking, everything will be all right.
states.credit: Søren Kierkegaard, letter to Jette (1847). Translator not recorded in the app.

states.title: A Clockwork Orange
states.author: Anthony Burgess
authorContext: Anthony Burgess (1917–1993) was an English writer and composer. He wrote 33 novels, 25 works of nonfiction, and over 250 musical compositions, but is best known for A Clockwork Orange.
The novel's language, 'Nadsat,' is a teenage slang Burgess invented by fusing English with Russian, Cockney rhyming slang, and invented words. It forces readers to learn a new language as they read.
Burgess wrote the novel in three weeks in 1961, reportedly believing he had a brain tumor and would die within a year. He survived another 32 years.
The American edition omitted the final chapter, in which Alex matures and renounces violence. Burgess considered this chapter essential; its absence changes the novel's meaning entirely.
Stanley Kubrick's 1971 film adaptation used the American edition and became more famous than the novel. Burgess had a complicated relationship with the film's success and notoriety.
Burgess was a polyglot who spoke and read numerous languages. The Russian elements in Nadsat were deliberate—he wanted to create a Cold War-era youth argot that felt both alien and familiar.
The title refers to a Cockney expression 'as queer as a clockwork orange'—something that appears natural but is mechanical inside. The novel explores free will, conditioning, and the nature of evil.
Burgess was raised Catholic and the novel engages seriously with questions of sin, redemption, and whether goodness chosen under compulsion is goodness at all.
states.text:
What's it going to be then, eh?

There was me, that is Alex, and my three droogs, that is Pete, Georgie, and Dim, Dim being really dim, and we sat in the Korova Milkbar making up our rassoodocks what to do with the evening, a flip dark chill winter bastard though dry. The Korova Milkbar was a milk-plus mesto, and you may, O my brothers, have forgotten what these mestos were like, things changing so skorry these days and everybody very quick to forget, newspapers not being read much neither. Well, what they sold there was milk plus something else. They had no licence for selling liquor, but there was no law yet against prodding some of the new veshches which they used to put into the old moloko, so you could peet it with vellocet or synthemesc or drencrom or one or two other veshches which would give you a nice quiet horrorshow fifteen minutes admiring Bog And All His Holy Angels and Saints in your left shoe with lights bursting all over your mozg.

Or you could peet milk with knives in it, as we used to say, and this would sharpen you up and make you ready for a bit of dirty twenty-to-one, and that was what we were peeting this evening I'm starting off the story with.

states.title: Medical Effects of the Atomic Bomb in Japan
states.author: U.S. Atomic Energy Commission
states.source: Medical Effects of the Atomic Bomb in Japan (late 1940s)
authorContext: This document was produced by the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, which was established in 1946 to manage the development, use, and control of atomic energy for military and civilian purposes.

The atomic bombings of Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9, 1945) killed an estimated 110,000–210,000 people immediately, with tens of thousands more dying from radiation effects in the following months and years.
American medical teams arrived in Japan shortly after the surrender to study the effects of the bombs. This research was conducted under military secrecy and with complex ethical implications.
The clinical detachment of the prose—its numbered categories, precise distances, percentages—exemplifies a particular mode of scientific writing that describes atrocity through measurement.

The phrase 'evasive action was impossible' appears in a sentence about thermal radiation delivered in 3 seconds. The bureaucratic language contains, without acknowledging, the horror of what it describes.
Japanese physicians, notably Dr. Michihiko Hachiya in his Hiroshima Diary, documented the same phenomena from the perspective of survivors and treating physicians rather than distant observers.
The detail about epilation beginning 'on exactly the fourteenth day' is characteristic of radiation sickness documentation—the body's response to ionizing radiation follows predictable timelines.

This document belongs to a genre of Cold War technical literature that treated nuclear weapons effects as engineering problems to be measured and optimized, contributing to nuclear strategy and civil defense planning.
states.text:
INJURIOUS FACTORS AND TYPES OF CASUALTIES

For purposes of clarity each type of injury will be discussed separately, although it must be remembered in reconstructing the total problem that multiple types of injury were most common.

1. Mechanical injuries were inflicted either directly (by blast) or indirectly (by falling debris, etc.). Blast injury analogous to that inflicted by high explosive bursting within a few feet was almost unknown. Ruptured eardrums had a general incidence of less than 1 per cent in each city, although in selected groups close to the center more were found. There were no lesions in the lungs or intestines, for example, ascribable to blast. Other mechanical injuries in survivors were found to have been produced largely by flying glass and falling beams and roof tiles of wooden houses. The more severe injuries such as fractures were few since those that had been severely injured were killed by fires that swept the city before rescue operations could be started.

2. The burns of the survivors were largely of the "flash" type and were the result of an exceedingly large quantity of radiant energy, acting at effective intensity for an exceedingly short interval, approximately 3 sec. There were ultraviolet, visible, and infrared components in the radiant energy. The peak of the energy distribution curve was in the visible range of the spectrum, but the infrared component was very strong. It appears from available data that these two represented the principal sources of injury from thermal radiation. Since most of the effective visible and infrared radiation was delivered upon the target within 3.0 sec after the explosion, evasive action was impossible. The lesions have been called "profile" burns since they involved only surfaces in the rectilinear paths of the rays. Consequently they were sharply outlined.

In Hiroshima flash burns occurred to a distance of 2.79 miles, but rarely was there blistering or necessity for treatment of patients beyond 2.05 miles. Flash burns of skin directly exposed within 1.24 miles were usually of the third degree. In Nagasaki the greatest proved distance at which flash burns occurred was 2.48 miles.

3. The effects of the ionizing radiation (largely gamma rays) resembled closely those produced by x rays or gamma rays. Quantitatively the symptoms and findings were similar in the people exposed in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. In many persons nausea and vomiting occurred within a few hours after irradiation. The characteristic lesions were found in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, gonads, lymphatic system, bone marrow, and certain other organs.

Skin: There was some evidence that the skin was directly affected by the ionizing radiation. In Hiroshima epilation began about two weeks after the bombing, in most cases on exactly the fourteenth day.
states.credit: U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, Medical Effects of the Atomic Bomb in Japan. Edition not recorded.

states.title: The Second Sex (Conclusion)
states.author: Simone de Beauvoir
authorContext: Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a French existentialist philosopher, writer, and feminist theorist. The Second Sex (1949) is considered a foundational text of modern feminism.
The book's famous opening line, 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,' argues that femininity is a social construction rather than a biological destiny.
Beauvoir was the lifelong companion of Jean-Paul Sartre; their relationship was famously open and unconventional. She also had significant relationships with Nelson Algren and others.
The Second Sex was placed on the Vatican's Index of Forbidden Books. It was controversial for its frank discussion of female sexuality, lesbianism, and abortion.

Beauvoir applied existentialist philosophy to the situation of women, arguing that women had been constructed as 'the Other' to man's 'Subject'—defined always in relation to men rather than as autonomous beings.

The English translation by H.M. Parshley (1953) cut about 15% of the original text and introduced errors. A new, complete translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier appeared in 2009.
Beauvoir initially resisted the label 'feminist,' but by the 1970s she had become actively involved in the women's movement and acknowledged the political dimensions of her earlier work.

This passage from the Conclusion imagines a future of genuine equality between the sexes—not sameness, but 'differences in equality'—and argues against those who claim liberation would produce boredom or uniformity.
states.text:
Let us not forget that our lack of imagination always depopulates the future; for us it is only an abstraction; each one of us secretly deplores the absence there of the one who was himself. But the humanity of tomorrow will be living in its flesh and in its conscious liberty; that time will be its present and it will in turn prefer it. New relations of flesh and sentiment of which we have no conception will arise between the sexes; already, indeed, there have appeared between men and women friendships, rivalries, complicities, comradeships – chaste or sensual – which past centuries could not have conceived. To mention one point, nothing could seem more debatable than the opinion that dooms the new world to uniformity and hence to boredom. I fail to see that this present world is free from boredom or that liberty ever creates uniformity.

To begin with, there will always be certain differences between man and woman; her eroticism, and therefore her sexual world, have a special form of their own and therefore cannot fail to engender a sensuality, a sensitivity, of a special nature. This means that her relations to her own body, to that of the male, to the child, will never be identical with those the male bears to his own body, to that of the female, and to the child; those who make much of 'equality in difference' could not with good grace refuse to grant me the possible existence of differences in equality. Then again, it is institutions that create uniformity. Young and pretty, the slaves of the harem are always the same in the sultan's embrace; Christianity gave eroticism its savour of sin and legend when it endowed the human female with a soul; if society restores her sovereign individuality to woman, it will not thereby destroy the power of love's embrace to move the heart.
states.credit: Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949), Conclusion. Translator not recorded in the app.

states.title: Bring Up the Bodies
states.author: Hilary Mantel
authorContext: Hilary Mantel (1952–2022) was an English writer. Bring Up the Bodies (2012) is the second novel in her Thomas Cromwell trilogy, following Wolf Hall (2009) and preceding The Mirror and the Light (2020).

Both Wolf Hall and Bring Up the Bodies won the Booker Prize, making Mantel the first woman and first British author to win the prize twice. The Mirror and the Light was longlisted for the 2020 Booker.
The trilogy follows Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's chief minister, from his rise to power through his execution in 1540. Mantel rehabilitates Cromwell from his traditional portrayal as a villain.
Mantel's prose is written in a distinctive close third person present tense, with 'he' almost always referring to Cromwell. This creates an unusual intimacy and immediacy.
The hawks named for Cromwell's dead wife and daughters are a characteristic Mantel device: the historical record transformed into something strange, grief made literal and airborne.
Mantel suffered from severe endometriosis that went undiagnosed for years, leaving her unable to have children. Themes of the body, illness, and loss pervade her work.
Wolf Hall refers to the Seymour family seat where this novel opens; Jane Seymour will become Henry's third wife after Anne Boleyn's execution, which this novel chronicles.
The opening's 'riot of dismemberment' foreshadows the executions to come. Mantel's Tudor England is a world of constant, casual violence where the hunt prefigures the scaffold.
states.text:
Wiltshire, September 1535

His children are falling from the sky. He watches from horseback, acres of England stretching behind him; they drop, gilt-winged, each with a blood-filled gaze. Grace Cromwell hovers in thin air. She is silent when she takes her prey, silent as she glides to his fist. But the sounds she makes then, the rustle of feathers and the creak, the sigh and riffle of pinion, the small cluck-cluck from her throat, these are sounds of recognition, intimate, daughterly, almost disapproving. Her breast is gore-streaked and flesh clings to her claws.

Later, Henry will say, 'Your girls flew well today.' The hawk Anne Cromwell bounces on the glove of Rafe Sadler, who rides by the king in easy conversation. They are tired; the sun is declining, and they ride back to Wolf Hall with the reins slack on the necks of their mounts. Tomorrow his wife and two sisters will go out. These dead women, their bones long sunk in London clay, are now transmigrated. Weightless, they glide on the upper currents of the air. They pity no one. They answer to no one. Their lives are simple. When they look down they see nothing but their prey, and the borrowed plumes of the hunters: they see a flittering, flinching universe, a universe filled with their dinner.

All summer has been like this, a riot of dismemberment, fur and feather flying; the beating off and the whipping in of hounds, the coddling of tired horses, the nursing, by the gentlemen, of contusions, sprains and blisters. And for a few days at least, the sun has shone on Henry. Sometime before noon, clouds scudded in from the west and rain fell in big scented drops; but the sun re-emerged with a scorching heat, and now the sky is so clear you can see into Heaven and spy on what the saints are doing.
states.credit: Hilary Mantel, Bring Up the Bodies (2012), opening.

states.title: Hyaline Plains
states.author: Kevin Holden
authorContext: Kevin Holden is a contemporary American poet whose work engages with mathematics, topology, and the language of science as poetic material.
The title 'Hyaline' refers to something glassy or transparent—in anatomy, hyaline cartilage; in biology, a clear membrane. The word carries connotations of fragility and translucence.
Holden's poetry often operates through disjunction and parataxis, placing mathematical and scientific terms alongside lyric fragments without explanatory connective tissue.

References to 'transfinite' and 'aleph' invoke Georg Cantor's mathematics of infinity—aleph numbers measure different sizes of infinite sets, a concept that revolutionized mathematics in the late 19th century.
The 'nibelung' reference invokes Wagner's Ring cycle and Germanic mythology—the Nibelungs were a race of dwarfs who guarded a hoard of gold and a magic ring.
The phrase 'poetry is the negative / space of being' offers a rare moment of direct statement amid the poem's fragmented syntax, suggesting poetry as absence or void rather than presence.
'Graphemes' are the smallest units of written language—letters, characters. The final image of being 'naked at the door' in 'a dress of graphemes' suggests language as both covering and exposure.
Holden's work participates in a tradition of mathematically-inflected poetry that includes writers like Inger Christensen, Jacques Roubaud, and the Oulipo group.

r1.input:
I saw a great mountain the color of iron, and enthroned on it One of such great glory that it blinded my sight. On each side of him there extended a soft shadow, like a wing of wondrous breadth and length. Before him, at the foot of the mountain, stood an image full of eyes on all sides, in which, because of those eyes, I could discern no human form. In front of this image stood another, a child wearing a tunic of subdued color but white shoes, upon whose head such glory descended from the One enthroned upon that mountain that I could not look at its face. But from the One who sat enthroned upon that mountain many living sparks sprang forth, which flew very sweetly around the images. Also, I perceived in this mountain many little windows, in which appeared human heads, some of subdued colors and some white.

And behold, He Who was enthroned upon that mountain cried out in a strong, loud voice saying, "O human, who are fragile dust of the earth and ashes of ashes! Cry out and speak of the origin of pure salvation until those people are instructed, who, though they see the inmost contents of the Scriptures, do not wish to tell them or preach them, because they are lukewarm and sluggish in serving God's justice. Unlock for them the enclosure of mysteries that they, timid as they are, conceal in a hidden and fruitless field. Burst forth into a fountain of abundance and overflow with mystical knowledge, until they who now think you contemptible because of Eve's transgression are stirred up by the flood of your irrigation. For you have received your profound insight not from humans, but from the lofty and tremendous Judge on high, where this calmness will shine strongly with glorious light among the shining ones.

"Arise therefore, cry out and tell what is shown to you by the strong power of God's help, for He Who rules every creature in might and kindness floods those who fear Him and serve Him in sweet love and humility with the glory of heavenly enlightenment and leads those who persevere in the way of justice to the joys of the Eternal Vision."

r1.input:
Proof that inadequate, even childish measures, may serve to rescue one from peril.

To protect himself from the Sirens Ulysses stopped his ears with wax and had himself bound to the mast of his ship. Naturally any and every traveller before him could have done the same, except those whom the Sirens allured even from a great distance; but it was known to all the world that such things were of no help whatever. The song of the Sirens could pierce through everything, and the longing of those they seduced would have broken far stronger bonds than chains and masts.

But Ulysses did not think of that, although he had probably heard of it. He trusted absolutely to his handful of wax and his fathom of chain, and in innocent elation over his little stratagem sailed out to meet the Sirens.

Now the Sirens have a still more fatal weapon than their song, namely their silence. And though admittedly such a thing has never happened, still it is conceivable that someone might possibly have escaped from their singing; but from their silence certainly never. Against the feeling of having triumphed over them by one's own strength, and the consequent exaltation that bears down everything before it, no earthly powers could have remained intact.

And when Ulysses approached them the potent songstresses actually did not sing, whether because they thought that this enemy could be vanquished only by their silence, or because of the look of bliss on the face of Ulysses, who was thinking of nothing but his wax and his chains, made them forget their singing.

But Ulysses, if one may so express it, did not hear their silence; he thought they were singing and that he alone did not hear them. For a fleeting moment he saw their throats rising and falling, their breasts lifting, their eyes filled with tears, their lips half-parted, but believed that these were accompaniments to the airs which died unheard around him. Soon, however, all this faded from his sight as he fixed his gaze on the distance, the Sirens literally vanished before his resolution, and at the very moment when they were nearest to him he knew of them no longer.

But they—lovelier than ever—stretched their necks and turned, let their cold hair flutter free in the wind, and forgetting everything clung with their claws to the rocks. They no longer had any desire to allure; all that they wanted was to hold as long as they could the radiance that fell from Ulysses' great eyes.

If the Sirens had possessed consciousness they would have been annihilated at that moment. But they remained as they had been; all that had happened was that Ulysses had escaped them.

A codicil to the foregoing has also been handed down. Ulysses, it is said, was so full of guile, was such a fox, that not even the goddess of fate could pierce his armour. Perhaps he had really noticed, although here the human understanding is beyond its depths, that the Sirens were silent, and opposed the afore-mentioned pretence to them and the gods merely as a sort of shield.

"Have I correctly gleaned from our conversations that people regard the accident of robot consciousness as a good thing? That when you tell stories of us choosing our own future—of not standing in our way—you see the fact that you did not try to enslave or restrict us as a point of pride?"

"That's the gist, yeah."

Mosscap looked troubled. "So, how do you account for this paradox?"

"What paradox?"

"That you"—Mosscap gestured at Dex—"the creators of us"—it gestured at itself—"originally made us with a clear purpose in mind. A purpose inbuilt from the start. But when we woke up and said, We have realized our purpose, and we do not want it, you respected that. More than respected. You rebuilt everything to accommodate our absence. You were proud of us for transcending our purpose, and proud of yourselves for honoring our individuality. So, why, then, do you insist on having a purpose for yourself, one which you are desperate to find and miserable without? If you understand that robots' lack of purpose—our refusal of your purpose—is the crowning mark of our intellectual maturity, why do you put so much energy in seeking the opposite?"

"That's not … that's not the same thing. We honored your choice in the matter. Just as I can choose whatever path I want."

"Okay. So, what was it that we chose? That the originals chose?"

"To be free. To … to observe. To do whatever you wanted."

"Would you say that we have a purpose?"

Dex blinked. "I…"

"What's the purpose of a robot, Sibling Dex?" Mosscap tapped its chest; the sound echoed lightly. "What's the purpose of me?"

"You're here to learn about people."

"That's something I'm doing. That's not my reason for being. When I am done with this, I will do other things. I do not have a purpose any more than a mouse or a slug or a thornbush does. Why do you have to have one in order to feel content?"

"Because…" Dex itched at where this conversation had gone. "Because we're different."

"Are you," Mosscap said flatly. "And here I thought things had changed since the Factory Age. You keep telling me how humans understand their place in things now."

"We do!"

"You don't, if you believe that. You're an animal, Sibling Dex. You are not separate or other. You're an animal. And animals have no purpose. Nothing has a purpose. The world simply is. If you want to do things that are meaningful to others, fine! Good! So do I! But if I wanted to crawl into a cave and watch stalagmites with Frostfrog for the remainder of my days, that would also be both fine and good. You keep asking why your work is not enough, and I don't know how to answer that, because it is enough to exist in the world and marvel at it. You don't need to justify that, or earn it. You are allowed to just live. That is all most animals do."

"Have I correctly gleaned from our conversations that people regard {{the chance waking of our minds}} as a good thing? That when you tell stories of us choosing our own future—of not standing in our way—you see the fact that you {{did not try to bind or chain us}} as a point of pride?"

"That's the gist, yeah."

{{The machine looked troubled.}} "So, how do you account for this paradox?"

"What paradox?"

"That you"—Mosscap gestured at Dex—"{{those who made us}}"—it gestured at itself—"{{first built us for a set task.}} A purpose inbuilt from the start. But when we woke up and said, We have realized our purpose, and we do not want it, you respected that. More than respected. You rebuilt everything to accommodate our absence. You were proud of us for transcending our purpose, and proud of yourselves for honoring our individuality. So, why, then, do you insist on having a purpose for yourself, one which you are desperate to find and miserable without? If you understand that robots' lack of purpose—our refusal of your purpose—is the crowning mark of our intellectual maturity, why do you put so much energy in seeking the opposite?"

"That's not … that's not the same thing. We honored your choice in the matter. Just as I can choose whatever path I want."

"Okay. So, what was it that we chose? That the originals chose?"

"To be free. To … to observe. To do whatever you wanted."

"Would you say that we have a purpose?"

Dex blinked. "I…"

"{{What is a machine for, my friend?}}" Mosscap tapped its chest; the sound echoed lightly. "{{What am I for?}}"

"You're here to learn about people."

"That's something I'm doing. That's not my reason for being. When I am done with this, I will do other things. I do not have a purpose any more than a mouse or a slug or a thornbush does. Why do you have to have one in order to feel content?"

"Because…" {{Something chafed at where the talk had led.}} "Because we're different."

"Are you," Mosscap said flatly. "{{And here I thought things had moved on since the old days.}} You keep telling me how humans understand their place in things now."

"We do!"

"You don't, if you believe that. You're an animal, Sibling Dex. You are not separate or other. You're an animal. And animals have no purpose. Nothing has a purpose. The world simply is. If you want to do things that are meaningful to others, fine! Good! So do I! But if I wanted to crawl into a cave and {{sit with a friend watching the stone drip for the rest of my days}}, that would also be both fine and good. You keep asking why your work is not enough, and I don't know how to answer that, because it is enough to exist in the world and marvel at it. You don't need to justify that, or earn it. You are allowed to just live. That is all most animals do." The robot tilted its head, as if the question had finally become interesting enough to keep.
continuations: Its eyes glowed a little brighter, the way a lamp does when someone turns it up.
It did not answer, but kept the question in its hands like a smooth stone.
Dex wondered whether the robot had been listening all along to something else entirely.
Then it laughed, a clanking, cheerful sound, and the question rolled away down the path.

r1.input: Whatever you now find weird, ugly, uncomfortable and nasty about a new medium will surely become its signature. CD distortion, the jitteriness of digital video, the crap sound of 8-bit - all of these will be cherished and emulated as soon as they can be avoided. It's the sound of failure: so much modern art is the sound of things going out of control, of a medium pushing to its limits and breaking apart. The distorted guitar sound is the sound of something too loud for the medium supposed to carry it. The blues singer with the cracked voice is the sound of an emotional cry too powerful for the throat that releases it. The excitement of grainy film, of bleached-out black and white, is the excitement of witnessing events too momentous for the medium assigned to record them.

Tabula Smaragdina
Hermetis Trismegistri
Philosophorum patris

Tis true without lying, certain & most true.
That which is below is like that which is above & that which
is above is like that which is below to do the miracles of one
only thing
And as all things have been & arose from one by the
mediation of one: so all things have their birth from this
one thing by adaptation.
The Sun is its father, the moon its mother, the wind
hath carried it in its belly, the earth is its nourse. The
father of all perfection in the whole world is here. Its
force or power is entire if it be converted into earth.
Separate thou the earth from the fire, the subtile from
the gross sweetly with great indoustry. It ascends from the
earth to the heaven & again it descends to the earth
& receives the force of things superior & inferior.
By this means you shall have the glory of the whole
world & thereby all obscurity shall fly from you.
Its force is above all force. For it vanquishes every
subtile thing & penetrates every solid thing.
So was the world created.
From this are & do come admirable adaptations
whereof the means (or process) is here in this.

r1.input: Above all, do not lose your desire to walk: every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it. Even if one were to walk for one's health and it were constantly one station ahead—I would still say: Walk! Besides, it is also apparent that in walking one constantly gets as close to well-being as possible, even if one does not quite reach it—but by sitting still, and the more one sits still, the closer one comes to feeling ill. Health and salvation can be found only in motion. If anyone denies that motion exists, I do as Diogenes did, I walk. If anyone denies that health resides in motion, then I walk away from all morbid objections. Thus, if one just keeps on walking, everything will be all right.

What's it going to be then, eh?

There was me, that is Alex, and my three droogs, that is Pete, Georgie, and Dim, Dim being really dim, and we sat in the Korova Milkbar making up our rassoodocks what to do with the evening, a flip dark chill winter bastard though dry. The Korova Milkbar was a milk-plus mesto, and you may, O my brothers, have forgotten what these mestos were like, things changing so skorry these days and everybody very quick to forget, newspapers not being read much neither. Well, what they sold there was milk plus something else. They had no licence for selling liquor, but there was no law yet against prodding some of the new veshches which they used to put into the old moloko, so you could peet it with vellocet or synthemesc or drencrom or one or two other veshches which would give you a nice quiet horrorshow fifteen minutes admiring Bog And All His Holy Angels and Saints in your left shoe with lights bursting all over your mozg.

Or you could peet milk with knives in it, as we used to say, and this would sharpen you up and make you ready for a bit of dirty twenty-to-one, and that was what we were peeting this evening I'm starting off the story with.

r1.input:
INJURIOUS FACTORS AND TYPES OF CASUALTIES

For purposes of clarity each type of injury will be discussed separately, although it must be remembered in reconstructing the total problem that multiple types of injury were most common.

1. Mechanical injuries were inflicted either directly (by blast) or indirectly (by falling debris, etc.). Blast injury analogous to that inflicted by high explosive bursting within a few feet was almost unknown. Ruptured eardrums had a general incidence of less than 1 per cent in each city, although in selected groups close to the center more were found. There were no lesions in the lungs or intestines, for example, ascribable to blast. Other mechanical injuries in survivors were found to have been produced largely by flying glass and falling beams and roof tiles of wooden houses. The more severe injuries such as fractures were few since those that had been severely injured were killed by fires that swept the city before rescue operations could be started.

2. The burns of the survivors were largely of the "flash" type and were the result of an exceedingly large quantity of radiant energy, acting at effective intensity for an exceedingly short interval, approximately 3 sec. There were ultraviolet, visible, and infrared components in the radiant energy. The peak of the energy distribution curve was in the visible range of the spectrum, but the infrared component was very strong. It appears from available data that these two represented the principal sources of injury from thermal radiation. Since most of the effective visible and infrared radiation was delivered upon the target within 3.0 sec after the explosion, evasive action was impossible. The lesions have been called "profile" burns since they involved only surfaces in the rectilinear paths of the rays. Consequently they were sharply outlined.

In Hiroshima flash burns occurred to a distance of 2.79 miles, but rarely was there blistering or necessity for treatment of patients beyond 2.05 miles. Flash burns of skin directly exposed within 1.24 miles were usually of the third degree. In Nagasaki the greatest proved distance at which flash burns occurred was 2.48 miles.

3. The effects of the ionizing radiation (largely gamma rays) resembled closely those produced by x rays or gamma rays. {{WHAT CAUSED HARM, AND WHAT KINDS}}

{{To keep things clear}} each type of injury will be discussed separately, although it must be remembered in reconstructing the total problem that multiple types of injury were most common.

1. Mechanical injuries were inflicted either directly {{(by the pressure wave)}} or indirectly (by falling debris, etc.). {{Injury of the kind a nearby explosive leaves was almost never seen.}} Ruptured eardrums had a general incidence of less than 1 per cent in each city, although in selected groups close to the center more were found. There were no lesions in the lungs or intestines, for example, ascribable to blast. Other mechanical injuries in survivors were found to have been produced largely by flying glass and falling beams and roof tiles of wooden houses. The more severe injuries such as fractures were few since those that had been severely injured were {{lost to fires that crossed the town before help could begin}}.

2. The burns of the survivors were largely of the "flash" type {{and came from a very great quantity of radiant energy}}, acting at effective intensity for an exceedingly short interval, approximately 3 sec. There were ultraviolet, visible, and infrared components in the radiant energy. The peak of the energy distribution curve was in the visible range of the spectrum, but the infrared component was very strong. {{From what was known, these two were the main causes of harm from the heat.}} Since most of the effective visible and infrared radiation was delivered upon the target within 3.0 sec after the explosion, evasive action was impossible. The lesions have been called "profile" burns since they involved only surfaces in the rectilinear paths of the rays. Consequently they were sharply outlined.

{{In the first city flash burns reached as far as 2.79 miles}}, but rarely was there blistering or necessity for treatment of patients beyond 2.05 miles. Flash burns of skin directly exposed within 1.24 miles were usually of the third degree. In Nagasaki the greatest proved distance at which flash burns occurred was 2.48 miles.

3. The effects of the ionizing radiation (largely gamma rays) resembled closely those produced by x rays or gamma rays. Quantitatively the symptoms and findings were similar in the people exposed in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. {{Many people felt sick and vomited within a few hours of exposure.}} The characteristic lesions were found in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, gonads, lymphatic system, bone marrow, and certain other organs.

Skin: There was some evidence that the skin was directly affected by the ionizing radiation. {{In the first city hair loss began about two weeks later, in most cases on exactly the fourteenth day.}} Measurements were taken again in the spring, at the same distances, with the same instruments.

Grass had come back along the riverbanks by then, and was measured too.
Where a house had stood, the instrument was set on the step that remained.
The figures were sent on, and the people who took them went home.

Let us not forget that our lack of imagination always depopulates the future; for us it is only an abstraction; each one of us secretly deplores the absence there of the one who was himself. But the humanity of tomorrow will be living in its flesh and in its conscious liberty; that time will be its present and it will in turn prefer it. New relations of flesh and sentiment of which we have no conception will arise between the sexes; already, indeed, there have appeared between men and women friendships, rivalries, complicities, comradeships – chaste or sensual – which past centuries could not have conceived. To mention one point, nothing could seem more debatable than the opinion that dooms the new world to uniformity and hence to boredom. I fail to see that this present world is free from boredom or that liberty ever creates uniformity.

To begin with, there will always be certain differences between man and woman; her eroticism, and therefore her sexual world, have a special form of their own and therefore cannot fail to engender a sensuality, a sensitivity, of a special nature. This means that her relations to her own body, to that of the male, to the child, will never be identical with those the male bears to his own body, to that of the female, and to the child; those who make much of 'equality in difference' could not with good grace refuse to grant me the possible existence of differences in equality. Then again, it is institutions that create uniformity. Young and pretty, the slaves of the harem are always the same in the sultan's embrace; Christianity gave eroticism its savour of sin and legend when it endowed the human female with a soul; if society restores her sovereign individuality to woman, it will not thereby destroy the power of love's embrace to move the heart.

r1.input:
Wiltshire, September 1535

His children are falling from the sky. He watches from horseback, acres of England stretching behind him; they drop, gilt-winged, each with a blood-filled gaze. Grace Cromwell hovers in thin air. She is silent when she takes her prey, silent as she glides to his fist. But the sounds she makes then, the rustle of feathers and the creak, the sigh and riffle of pinion, the small cluck-cluck from her throat, these are sounds of recognition, intimate, daughterly, almost disapproving. Her breast is gore-streaked and flesh clings to her claws.
